Raymond III Count of Tripoli also known as Raymond of Antioch was a nobleman from the Crusader states in the Levant He was the count of Tripoli from 1152 until his death in 1187 He was the son of Raymond II Count of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem He was born around 1140 and died on February 29 1187 He was married twice first to Eschiva of Bures with whom he had two sons and a daughter and then to Hawisa of Tabaria with whom he had two sons and three daughters

Raymond III was involved in the politics of the Crusader states throughout his life In 1152 he succeeded his father as count of Tripoli and quickly became embroiled in the power struggles of the region He allied himself with the Byzantine Empire against the forces of Nur ad-Din the Muslim ruler of Aleppo and Damascus In 1158 he played a key role in the defense of the County of Tripoli against an attack by Nur ad-Din's forces

In 1164 Raymond III was captured by Nur ad-Din during the Battle of Harim and held prisoner for six years He was released in 1170 and returned to Tripoli where he continued to rule as count He maintained close ties with the Kingdom of Jerusalem and was involved in its politics During the reign of King Baldwin IV he served as regent of the kingdom on several occasions

In 1183 Raymond III became involved in a power struggle with Guy of Lusignan the husband of Sibylla of Jerusalem the sister of Baldwin IV Raymond III opposed Guy's election as king of Jerusalem and supported the claims of Baldwin V instead However when Baldwin V died in 1185 Raymond III accepted Guy as king

Raymond III died on February 29 1187 during the Battle of Cresson against the forces of Saladin the Muslim ruler of Egypt and Syria His death marked the beginning of the end for the Crusader states in the Levant Within a year Saladin had conquered Jerusalem and the other Crusader states had been reduced to a few isolated strongholds Raymond III's legacy as a nobleman and leader of the Crusader states is mixed Some historians view him as a capable and effective ruler while others see him as a divisive figure who contributed to the decline of the Crusader states.

*Early life and family*
-----------------------

Raymond III was born around 1140, the son of Raymond II Count of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem. He had two brothers, Bohemond III and Bertrand, and a sister, Melisende. Raymond III was married twice, first to Eschiva of Bures with whom he had two sons and a daughter, and then to Hawisa of Tabaria with whom he had two sons and three daughters.

*Politics of the Crusader states*
----------------------------------

Raymond III was involved in the politics of the Crusader states throughout his life. In 1152, he succeeded his father as count of Tripoli and quickly became embroiled in the power struggles of the region. He allied himself with the Byzantine Empire against the forces of Nur ad-Din the Muslim ruler of Aleppo and Damascus. In 1158, he played a key role in the defense of the County of Tripoli against an attack by Nur ad-Din's forces.

In 1164, Raymond III was captured by Nur ad-Din during the Battle of Harim and held prisoner for six years. He was released in 1170 and returned to Tripoli where he continued to rule as count. He maintained close ties with the Kingdom of Jerusalem and was involved in its politics. During the reign of King Baldwin IV, he served as regent of the kingdom on several occasions.

In 1183, Raymond III became involved in a power struggle with Guy of Lusignan the husband of Sibylla of Jerusalem the sister of Baldwin IV. Raymond III opposed Guy's election as king of Jerusalem and supported the claims of Baldwin V instead. However, when Baldwin V died in 1185, Raymond III accepted Guy as king.

*Legacy*
--------

Raymond III died on February 29, 1187, during the Battle of Cresson against the forces of Saladin the Muslim ruler of Egypt and Syria. His death marked the beginning of the end for the Crusader states in the Levant. Within a year, Saladin had conquered Jerusalem and the other Crusader states had been reduced to a few isolated strongholds.

Raymond III's legacy as a nobleman and leader of the Crusader states is mixed. Some historians view him as a capable and effective ruler, while others see him as a divisive figure who contributed to the decline of the Crusader states. Despite the controversies surrounding his life and career, Raymond III remains an important figure in the history of the Crusader states in the Levant.
